one_liner: Lazy, ALTREP-backed delimited-file reader for R; indexes then reads on demand, beating base R's read.delim/readr/data.table.
what_it_does: Reads and writes CSV/TSV/fixed-width text into R data frames/tibbles. Instead of parsing every value up front, vroom does one fast indexing pass over the file to record each field's byte offsets, then returns ALTREP vectors that materialize a column's actual values only when they are first accessed. Its API mirrors readr::read_delim (col_types, col_select, multi-file and multi-connection input), so most readr code ports with a function-name swap rather than a rewrite.
how_it_is_fast: Memory-maps the input file (bundled mio C++ library) and scans it with multiple threads to build a byte-offset index of every delimited field, so no value is parsed before it's needed. Returned columns are R ALTREP objects (character columns lazy by default) that convert raw bytes to R values only on access; non-character materialization and file writing also run multi-threaded, and grisu3 provides fast double-to-string formatting when writing.
when_to_use: Large local, uncompressed CSV/TSV/FWF files (hundreds of MB to multi-GB) read directly from disk, where memory-mapping applies
Pipelines that only touch a subset of rows/columns after loading (select/filter before printing or string ops), so lazy character materialization pays off
Existing readr users who want a faster, largely drop-in replacement without rewriting column-spec code
Writing large delimited files, where parallel formatting plus async write beats base R's write functions
R >= 4.1 environments, where ALTREP is fully supported by the runtime
when_not_to_use: Small files, where indexing overhead and R startup cost dominate and base read.delim/readr are already fast enough

Workflows that immediately print, filter, or string-process every character column, since that forces materialization and shifts most of the 'read' cost to first access, hiding behind read-time-only benchmarks
Remote or compressed sources (.gz/.bz2/.xz/.zip): vroom downloads to a temp file before mapping it, losing the mmap/lazy advantage
Contexts needing embedded newlines inside quoted headers/fields, which force num_threads = 1 and remove the multi-threaded indexing speedup
Situations requiring reproducible cross-hardware speedup numbers: the cited benchmarks give no compiler flags, and only the newer vignette names a CPU (EC2 m5.4xlarge)

integration.dependencies: R packages bit64, cli, glue, hms, lifecycle, rlang, tibble, tidyselect, tzdb, vctrs, withr (Imports); cpp11, progress, tzdb (LinkingTo, compile-time); bundled mio (header-only C++ mmap library)
integration.min_toolchain: R >= 4.1 (Depends, needed for full ALTREP support); C++ compiler to build from source (CRAN also ships binaries)
integration.platforms: any platform R runs on (Windows/macOS/Linux, x86-64/aarch64) via mio's cross-platform mmap wrapper
integration.thread_safety: not documented for concurrent R sessions/threads calling vroom simultaneously; internally spawns VROOM_THREADS worker threads (default parallel::detectCores()) for indexing, materialization, and writing
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the baseline here is base R read.delim, and vroom's call signature is different (readr-style, not read.delim/read.csv-style); switching requires touching read calls, though the tibble result behaves like a data frame

gotchas: Only character columns use ALTREP lazy loading by default (VROOM_USE_ALTREP_CHR=true); numeric/integer/date ALTREP is opt-in via separate env vars, so headline read-time numbers can hide deferred character-materialization cost
Reading from R connections or compressed/remote files downloads to a temp file first, forfeiting the mmap-based lazy-read advantage
Embedded newlines inside quoted headers or fields require num_threads = 1, disabling the multi-threaded indexing that produces most of the speedup
Repository moved from r-lib/vroom to tidyverse/vroom in April 2022; the r-lib URL still resolves via GitHub's redirect
pick_this_over_siblings_when: All catalogued siblings target C/Go/Rust/.NET/Ruby/Python CSV stacks; vroom is the only R-ecosystem entry, so pick it whenever the pipeline is already in R and you want readr-compatible syntax — its speed claim is against base R's read.delim, not against any sibling's baseline, so it isn't a substitute for those language-specific choices.
verified_claims_summary: On a real 1.53GB/14.7M-row/11-column taxi-trip CSV, the tidyverse blog table reports vroom reading in 3.6s versus base R read.delim's 1m21.5s (~22.6x), and a full read+print+head+tail+sample+filter+summarise workflow at 7s versus 1m22.6s (~11.8x); the post gives no CPU or compiler flags. A newer benchmarks vignette (vroom 1.5.1, public code in inst/bench/taxi, EC2 m5.4xlarge/16 vCPUs) shows read.delim at 1m12.3s versus vroom 1.3s to read, still without compiler flags.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-06-09, current CRAN release 1.7.1, part of the core tidyverse); MIT-licensed (DESCRIPTION and LICENSE.md) and simple to depend on via CRAN or pak, despite GitHub's NOASSERTION license auto-detection.
